oldWorld.title: The Old World
oldWorld.subtitle: Ancestral Disciplines
oldWorld.about: The Old World holds seventy years of AI research that came together in the 2020s. Its provinces grew up as separate fields: symbolic AI reasoned with explicit rules and search, information retrieval ranked documents, reinforcement learning learned from reward, and neural networks, from the perceptron to backpropagation, learned patterns from data. For decades the neural line was a minority view. That changed in the 2010s, when large datasets, GPUs and a few key tricks made deep networks win, first in vision with AlexNet and then in language with word vectors, LSTMs and attention. The Transformer (2017) made training parallel enough to scale, and pretraining plus scaling laws turned it into the large language models that the New World is built on. Many Old World ideas are being rediscovered there: retrieval feeds RAG, RL trains reasoning models, search guides agents, and imitation learning trains robots.

territories.subtitle: Information Retrieval
territories.about: Information retrieval is the old craft of finding the few documents that matter in a huge collection. It began with library indexing and the statistical idea that rare words carry the most meaning (TF-IDF, 1972), which led to the BM25 scoring function still used by Elasticsearch today. Web search added learning to rank: models that combine hundreds of signals to order results. Two threads from this province run straight into today's RAG systems. Open-domain question answering showed that you can answer questions by first retrieving passages and then reading them with a neural model. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes made it practical to search millions of embedding vectors in milliseconds, and they are the engine inside every vector database. Most of retrieval-augmented generation is this province's machinery with an LLM as the reader.

learningPath.title: Tf-idf weighting
learningPath.by: Manning, Raghavan & Schütze (Introduction to Information Retrieval)
learningPath.why: The textbook starting point: how weighting words by rarity turned keyword matching into ranking. Short, with the formulas you will see everywhere after.

learningPath.title: Practical BM25 - Part 2: The BM25 Algorithm and its Variables
learningPath.why: Walks through BM25 term by term, including what k1 and b actually do. This is still the default scorer in Elasticsearch and the sparse half of most hybrid RAG search.

learningPath.title: 3 Vector-based Methods for Similarity Search (TF-IDF, BM25, SBERT)
learningPath.why: Implements TF-IDF, BM25 and sentence-embedding search side by side in Python. It shows how sparse retrieval relates to the dense vectors used today.

learningPath.title: Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds (HNSW)
learningPath.why: Explains, with diagrams, the graph index inside most vector databases. It shows why searching millions of embeddings takes milliseconds.

learningPath.title: How to Build an Open-Domain Question Answering System?
learningPath.why: A survey of the retriever-reader systems (DrQA, DPR, REALM, RAG) that link classic search to today's retrieval-augmented generation.

territories.subtitle: Deep Learning and NLP
territories.about: This is the province where the explosion was built. It starts with the perceptron (1958) and backpropagation (1986), the methods that made layered neural networks trainable, and with Shannon's idea that language can be modeled by predicting the next word. For decades language was handled with counts and probabilities: n-gram models, hidden Markov models for speech, and statistical machine translation. The neural turn came in steps: neural language models (2003), the deep-learning revival (2006), word2vec's word vectors (2013), and LSTM encoder-decoders with attention for translation (2014). The Transformer (2017) dropped recurrence for pure attention, which made training parallel enough to scale. Pretraining on huge text corpora (GPT and BERT, 2018) and scaling laws (2020) turned that architecture into today's LLMs. The province also holds the architecture choices engineers still make: mixture of experts, state-space models, rotary positions and sparse attention.

learningPath.title: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
learningPath.why: Builds a character-level language model from bigram counts up to a trained neural net, in code. You see what predicting the next token actually means before any of the history.

learningPath.title: The Illustrated Word2vec
learningPath.why: Shows how words became vectors learned from context. The idea of an embedding runs through everything that came after, including today's vector search.

learningPath.title: Visualizing A Neural Machine Translation Model (Mechanics of Seq2seq Models With Attention)
learningPath.why: Animates the encoder-decoder RNNs of 2014 and the attention step bolted onto them. It makes clear which problem the Transformer was built to solve.

learningPath.title: Attention Is All You Need
learningPath.why: The paper that dropped recurrence and kept only attention. It is short and readable once the previous steps make sense.

learningPath.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
learningPath.why: Writes a small GPT line by line and trains it. It ties the earlier pieces (tokens, embeddings, attention) into the model shape every LLM uses today.

territories.subtitle: Symbolic AI and Planning
territories.about: Before learning dominated, AI meant explicit reasoning: represent the problem in symbols and search for a solution. This province holds that tradition. Heuristic search (A*, 1968) explores the most promising paths first. Theorem proving (1965) mechanized logic and led to Prolog and formal verification. STRIPS (1971) described actions by preconditions and effects, the basis of classical planning and of the PDDL standard. Expert systems captured specialist knowledge as rules and gave AI its first commercial boom in the 1980s, then its first winter when they proved brittle. Monte Carlo tree search (2006) cracked Go-playing programs, and multi-agent systems research worked out how autonomous agents coordinate. Much of this has come back: LLM agents call tools like expert-system modules, reasoning methods search over generated steps, and LLM+planner systems hand problems to PDDL solvers.

learningPath.title: The Quest for Artificial Intelligence
learningPath.why: A free history of AI written by an author of A* and STRIPS. Its chapters on search, Shakey and expert systems give the context for this whole province.

learningPath.title: Introduction to the A* Algorithm
learningPath.why: An interactive explanation of breadth-first search, Dijkstra and A*. Heuristic search is the idea most of this province builds on.

learningPath.title: Shakey: Experiments in Robot Planning and Learning (1972)
learningPath.why: The original SRI film of the robot that A* and STRIPS were invented for. It shows plan-then-act agents years before LLM agents.

learningPath.title: Hands-on-Introduction (via PDDL) to Automated Planning
learningPath.why: An introduction to classical planning that assumes no background. You write PDDL domains and run a planner on them, the same setup LLM+P-style agents use today.

learningPath.title: A Survey of Monte Carlo Tree Search Methods
learningPath.why: The standard reference on MCTS, the search method behind AlphaGo and much recent test-time search over LLM reasoning.

territories.subtitle: Reinforcement Learning
territories.about: Reinforcement learning is learning from reward rather than from labeled examples: an agent acts, sees what happens, and adjusts. Its mathematical frame, the Markov decision process, dates to Bellman's dynamic programming in the 1950s. Two families of methods grew from it. Value-based methods such as Q-learning (1989–92) learn how good each action is. Policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, 1992; actor-critic, 1999) adjust the policy directly. Deep learning joined in 2013, when DQN learned Atari games from pixels, and AlphaGo (2016) combined deep networks, self-play and tree search to beat a Go champion. PPO (2017) became the stable, simple default. This province hands the New World its training machinery: RLHF, RL with verifiable rewards and reasoning-model training are all policy-gradient methods applied to language models.

learningPath.title: Part 1: Key Concepts in RL
learningPath.why: A short, code-minded introduction to the RL vocabulary (states, policies, returns, value functions) used by RLHF and RLVR papers.

learningPath.title: RL Course by David Silver - Lecture 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
learningPath.why: The first lecture of the most widely watched RL course, given by AlphaGo's lead researcher. The later lectures cover MDPs, Q-learning and policy gradients in order.

learningPath.title: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd edition)
learningPath.by: Richard S. Sutton & Andrew G. Barto
learningPath.why: The field's textbook, free online. Read chapters 3 (MDPs), 6 (TD and Q-learning) and 13 (policy gradients) for the background to RLHF.

learningPath.title: Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning
learningPath.why: The Nature DQN paper, where a neural network learned 49 Atari games from pixels. It started the deep RL era.

learningPath.title: AlphaGo - The Movie | Full award-winning documentary
learningPath.why: The story of the 2016 match against Lee Sedol, which put learned policies combined with search into the public eye.

territories.subtitle: Knowledge Representation
territories.about: Knowledge representation asks how to store what a machine knows so that it can reason with it. Semantic networks (1968) drew knowledge as a graph of concepts and labeled relations, and frames, ontologies and the Semantic Web's RDF and OWL followed. Bayesian networks (1988) added uncertainty, attaching probabilities to the links so a system can reason from evidence to likely causes. Google's Knowledge Graph (2012) brought large entity graphs into everyday products, and Wikidata and enterprise graphs followed. Neural networks overtook hand-built knowledge for most tasks, but structured knowledge is back in the New World: GraphRAG builds knowledge graphs from documents to answer questions that span them, and agents query graphs and databases for facts a model shouldn't guess.

learningPath.title: What is a Knowledge Representation?
learningPath.by: Randall Davis, Howard Shrobe & Peter Szolovits
learningPath.why: A classic essay on what a representation commits you to. It is useful background for thinking about structured memory and tool schemas for LLMs.

learningPath.title: Semantic Networks
learningPath.why: An encyclopedia survey of nodes-and-links knowledge, from Quillian's semantic memory to frames and conceptual graphs.

learningPath.title: Introduction to Semantic Networks - Georgia Tech - KBAI: Part1
learningPath.why: A short lecture that builds a semantic network by hand, so the idea is concrete before reading about knowledge graphs at scale.

learningPath.title: Knowledge Graphs
learningPath.why: The comprehensive modern survey: data models, schemas, reasoning, embeddings and how enterprise KGs are built. It is the background for GraphRAG.

learningPath.title: The History of Wikidata
learningPath.why: Wikidata's creator tells how the largest open knowledge graph was built. It is one of the structured sources LLMs are now grounded on.

territories.subtitle: Human-Computer Interaction
territories.about: This province holds the AI side of how people work with computers. ELIZA (1966) was the first chatbot, and its users' readiness to confide in a few pattern-matching rules was an early warning about how easily people credit machines with understanding. Dialogue systems and voice assistants carried the idea forward for decades. Mixed-initiative interaction (1999) asked when an assistant should act on its own, ask first, or stay quiet, weighing its uncertainty against the cost of interrupting. Both ideas are now everywhere in the New World: chat is the default interface to LLMs, and copilots, approval prompts and agent check-ins are mixed-initiative design problems. Classic HCI that isn't AI, such as direct manipulation, appears on the map only as an external ancestor.

learningPath.title: The Chatbot Inventor’s Cautionary Alert (1978)
learningPath.why: ELIZA's creator, in his own words, on why people's readiness to confide in a simple program alarmed him.

learningPath.title: ELIZA Reinterpreted: The world's first chatbot was not intended as a chatbot at all
learningPath.why: A recent history, drawing on the recovered original code, of what ELIZA was actually for and how it became the archetypal chatbot.

learningPath.title: Mixed-initiative interaction
learningPath.by: James Allen, Curry Guinn & Eric Horvitz
learningPath.why: A short framing of when the human or the machine should take the lead in a dialogue. It is the core question in designing copilots and agents.

learningPath.title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
learningPath.why: Microsoft's 18 tested guidelines, drawn from two decades of mixed-initiative research. They are a practical checklist for AI product UX.

learningPath.title: KDD2023 - Keynote: People and Machines: Pathways to Deeper Human-AI Synergy
learningPath.why: The originator of mixed-initiative interfaces revisits its principles for the LLM era, covering who acts when, complementarity and grounding.

territories.subtitle: Computer Vision
territories.about: Computer vision is where deep learning first proved itself. Convolutional networks (1989) built in the fact that an object looks the same wherever it appears in an image, and read handwritten zip codes for the US Postal Service. The field's turning point came in 2012, when AlexNet, trained on GPUs over the ImageNet dataset, beat every hand-engineered system by a wide margin and set off the deep-learning era. Residual networks (2015) made networks hundreds of layers deep, and their shortcut connections are in every Transformer. Generative models grew here too: variational autoencoders (2013) and GANs (2014) were the first deep networks that could draw. The Vision Transformer (2020) then showed images could be handled as sequences of patches, which let vision and language share one architecture.

learningPath.title: How we teach computers to understand pictures
learningPath.why: The ImageNet story from the person who built it. It explains why a big labeled dataset was the missing ingredient for deep learning in vision.

learningPath.title: Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now
learningPath.why: Reproduces LeCun's 1989 convolutional net in modern PyTorch and asks what changed since. It shows that the architecture barely moved and that data and compute did the rest.

learningPath.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
learningPath.by: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever & Geoffrey Hinton
learningPath.why: AlexNet, the 2012 result that convinced the field. Reading it shows how much of the modern recipe (GPUs, ReLU, dropout, data augmentation) was already there.

learningPath.title: Lecture 9 | CNN Architectures
learningPath.why: Walks through AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet and ResNet in order. You see why each design appeared and why residual connections stuck.

learningPath.title: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
learningPath.why: Explains how cutting an image into patches let a plain Transformer replace convolutions. This is where vision joined the same architecture as language models.

territories.subtitle: Robotics and Control
territories.about: Robotics is the oldest test of AI in the physical world, and the hardest, because mistakes compound and real trials are slow and expensive. This province holds the ideas that today's robot foundation models inherited. Behavior cloning (ALVINN, 1989) taught a vehicle to steer by imitating a human driver, and showed both the promise and the weakness of imitation: small errors drift into situations the demonstrations never covered. DAgger (2010) fixed that drift by asking the expert to correct the learner in the states it actually reaches. Fast physics simulators such as MuJoCo (2012) let robots practice millions of times in software before touching hardware. Imitation learning, interactive correction and simulation are still the core of robot learning, and DAgger's idea reappears in on-policy distillation of LLMs.

learningPath.title: CS 285: Lecture 2, Imitation Learning. Part 1
learningPath.why: Opens Berkeley's deep RL course with behavior cloning, the supervised imitation recipe that SFT on demonstrations repeats for language models.

learningPath.title: Imitation Learning Tutorial ICML 2018
learningPath.why: A two-hour tutorial covering behavior cloning, why it compounds errors, and interactive fixes like DAgger.

learningPath.title: An Algorithmic Perspective on Imitation Learning
learningPath.why: A survey of imitation learning for robotics that organizes behavior cloning, DAgger and inverse RL into one framework.

learningPath.title: Opening up a physics simulator for robotics
learningPath.why: Why MuJoCo became the standard simulator for learning control, and why DeepMind made it free and open source.

learningPath.title: End to End Learning for Self-Driving Cars
learningPath.why: NVIDIA's revival of ALVINN's idea with a deep CNN. It shows behavior cloning from pixels working on real roads.

territories.title: The Engine Works
territories.subtitle: Inference and Serving
territories.about:
Inference and serving is the work of running a trained model fast and cheaply. The central fact is that generating text is limited by memory, not arithmetic: a model writes one token at a time, and each step has to read all of its weights plus a KV cache holding attention state for every earlier token. The cache grows with context length and with every concurrent request, and much of this region is about fitting, sharing and shrinking it.

Serving engines solved the basic problems first. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave a batch at every step so the GPU never idles, PagedAttention stores the cache in small blocks like virtual memory so little is wasted, and FlashAttention computes attention without moving large matrices through slow memory. Quantization stores weights, and then the cache, in fewer bits, which also makes models small enough for laptops and phones. Speculative decoding has a fast drafter guess several tokens that the big model checks at once.

The current stack treats the KV cache as data to manage across a cluster. Prompt caching reuses it for shared prefixes, and providers bill cache hits as cheaper input tokens. Chunked prefill keeps long prompts from stalling other users, and disaggregated serving runs prompt processing and token generation on separate machines, shipping the cache between them and offloading it to CPU memory or SSD for reuse. From the application side the main levers are routing easy requests to cheaper models, ordering prompts so caches hit, and constrained decoding for guaranteed output formats. Landmarks worth knowing: the KV cache, continuous batching, PagedAttention, FlashAttention, quantization, speculative decoding and prompt caching. The open questions are mostly economic: how to trade time to first token, streaming speed and cost per token across very different workloads, long-running agents especially.

learningPath.title: Transformer Inference Arithmetic
learningPath.why: Works through the memory and compute math of generating one token at a time. It shows why decoding is limited by memory bandwidth and why the KV cache is the main thing to manage.

learningPath.title: Achieve 23x LLM Inference Throughput & Reduce p50 Latency
learningPath.why: Explains continuous batching and why paged KV memory makes it work. Read it to see how serving engines keep the GPU busy across many requests.

learningPath.title: A Visual Guide to Quantization
learningPath.why: Illustrated tour of number formats and the main weight quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF). It covers the most common way to fit a model into less memory.

learningPath.title: Looking back at speculative decoding
learningPath.by: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias (Google Research)
learningPath.why: The original authors explain how a cheap draft model plus one verification pass speeds up decoding without changing outputs. Start here before draft heads like EAGLE and Medusa.

learningPath.title: Fast and Expressive LLM Inference with RadixAttention and SGLang
learningPath.by: Lianmin Zheng, Ying Sheng et al. (LMSYS)
learningPath.why: Shows how reusing the KV cache across requests that share a prefix saves recomputation. This is the mechanism behind prefix and prompt caching.

learningPath.title: DistServe: disaggregating prefill and decoding for goodput-optimized LLM inference
learningPath.why: Explains why prefill and decode have different bottlenecks and why large deployments now run them on separate GPUs. It ties the earlier pieces into the shape of a modern serving stack.

territories.title: The Whispering Coast
territories.subtitle: Prompting and Context Engineering
territories.about:
Prompting and Context Engineering is about shaping what a model does purely through what you send it, without touching its weights. It began as prompt engineering: finding instructions and examples that got a pretrained model to do a task. As models went into products, prompts became software: templates, chains, system prompts, and schema-shaped outputs that code can parse.

Two branches grew from there. Programmatic optimization stops hand-tuning: methods like APE, DSPy and TextGrad generate and score prompt variants against a dataset and a metric, so prompts become compiled artifacts gated by evals. Context engineering arrived with agents: once a model runs for hundreds of turns with tools, the question shifts from how to word an instruction to what should be in the context window at all. Long windows didn't remove the problem, since models still miss material buried in the middle, so compaction, careful ordering, and progressive disclosure keep the working set small and relevant.

Landmarks worth knowing: few-shot prompting, structured outputs, declarative prompt compilation, and context engineering. The direction of travel is from writing prompts to engineering the whole input state, measured by evals.

learningPath.title: Prompt Engineering
learningPath.why: A compact map of the basic techniques (zero-/few-shot, example selection, chain-of-thought, automatic prompt design), with the papers behind each, before you go deeper on any one.

learningPath.title: Prompting 101 | Code w/ Claude
learningPath.why: Watch a production prompt get built and debugged step by step: system prompt, task context, examples, output format.

learningPath.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
learningPath.why: The experiment that showed where you put information in a long context changes whether the model uses it, which is why context engineering became its own discipline.

learningPath.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
learningPath.why: Shifts the question from wording one prompt to curating everything an agent sees over many turns: compaction, note-taking, sub-agents and just-in-time retrieval.

learningPath.title: Let the LLM Write the Prompts: An Intro to DSPy in Compound AI Pipelines
learningPath.why: A 30-minute practitioner case for treating prompts as optimizable parameters, showing a real pipeline improved with an optimizer instead of hand-tuning.

learningPath.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
learningPath.why: The formal version of that idea: signatures, modules and a compiler that bootstraps demonstrations and instructions against a metric.

territories.title: The Archival Reach
territories.subtitle: Retrieval and Knowledge
territories.about:
Retrieval and Knowledge covers how AI systems bring outside facts into the model's context, so answers rest on your documents rather than on what the model memorized. It grew out of classical search (BM25 keyword ranking) and neural embeddings, and took its modern shape in 2020 with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find relevant passages, put them in the prompt, generate.

The basic pipeline of chunk, embed and retrieve fails in predictable ways, and most of the region is fixes for them. Chunks lose their surrounding context, so contextual retrieval, late chunking and parent-document retrieval put it back. A single embedding vector blurs exact terms and fine detail, so production systems combine keyword and vector search, rerank candidates with a cross-encoder, and sometimes keep one vector per token (late interaction). Bad retrieval poisons the answer, so newer designs grade what they retrieved, retrieve again mid-answer, or hand search to an agent that issues its own queries, including grep and file reads over code.

Two debates shape the region today. Million-token context windows did not make retrieval obsolete: models get distracted by irrelevant material in long contexts, and sending everything costs far more per query, so systems increasingly choose between retrieval and long context per question. Graph-based retrieval answers global, multi-hop questions that passage search can't, but full GraphRAG indexing is expensive, and lighter variants defer most of the work to query time. Landmarks worth knowing: embeddings and dense retrieval, RAG, hybrid search with reranking, contextual retrieval, and agentic RAG.

learningPath.title: Stanford CS25: V3 I Retrieval Augmented Language Models
learningPath.why: One of the RAG paper's authors explains why a model's frozen weights go stale and make things up, and how pairing it with a retriever addresses both. A good map of the whole region before the details.

learningPath.title: Embeddings: What they are and why they matter
learningPath.why: A plain-language walk through what an embedding is and how similarity search over embeddings works, with runnable examples. This is the building block under dense retrieval.

learningPath.title: Beyond the Basics of Retrieval for Augmenting Generation (w/ Ben Clavié)
learningPath.by: Ben Clavié (Mastering LLMs conference, hosted by Hamel Husain)
learningPath.why: Lays out the production baseline step by step: keyword search alongside embeddings, a cross-encoder reranker on top, and where late-interaction models fit. Explains why a single vector search is rarely enough.

learningPath.title: Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems
learningPath.why: Measures how much each layer of the baseline helps (BM25 plus embeddings, then reranking) and adds one cheap fix: prefixing each chunk with a short note on where it came from before indexing.

learningPath.title: Long Context RAG Performance of LLMs
learningPath.why: Tests whether stuffing more retrieved text into long-context models keeps helping. Most models peak and then decline, which is the practical answer to 'do we still need retrieval?'

learningPath.title: The unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for agentic search — Jo Kristian Bergum, Hornet.dev
learningPath.why: When an agent writes its own search queries, they get longer and more specific, and plain keyword search becomes a strong tool again. A useful counterweight as retrieval moves inside agent loops.

territories.title: The Free Cities
territories.subtitle: Agents and Orchestration
territories.about:
Agents and Orchestration covers models that act: calling tools, running in loops, remembering across sessions, and working with other agents. It began with routing. MRKL sent parts of a request to calculators and APIs, Toolformer trained models to decide when to call tools themselves, and function calling made that a standard API: the model returns a structured call, your code runs it. ReAct wrapped this in the basic agent loop of think, act, observe, repeat.

Fully autonomous loops proved expensive and unpredictable in production, so most deployed systems moved back toward workflows: control flow written in code, with the model called only where judgment is needed. Autonomy survives where tasks are open-ended and the environment is safe to explore, above all in coding agents, which now run for hours across many context windows using progress files, memory, and subagents.

Protocols turned tools into shared infrastructure. MCP lets one server work with any client, Agent Skills package know-how an agent loads on demand, and code execution keeps bulky tool results out of the context window. Landmarks worth knowing: function calling, the ReAct loop, workflow graphs, MCP, and coding agents. The direction of travel is toward bounded, well-instrumented agents rather than unconstrained autonomy.

learningPath.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
learningPath.why: One map of the whole field (planning, memory, tool use) with the papers behind each part, so the later readings have somewhere to land.

learningPath.title: LLM Agents: History & Overview (UC Berkeley CS294-196)
learningPath.why: The ReAct author explains how agents grew out of reasoning plus acting, which is the loop every later system still runs.

learningPath.title: Building effective agents
learningPath.why: Separates workflows (control flow in code) from agents (the model chooses the steps) and names the common patterns, which is the main design choice you will face in practice.

learningPath.title: Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents
learningPath.why: Most agent failures trace back to tool design, and this covers naming, scoping, response size and how to evaluate tools.

learningPath.title: Building Agents with Model Context Protocol - Full Workshop
learningPath.why: Shows how tools become shared infrastructure through MCP, walking through servers, clients and how an agent uses them.

learningPath.title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
learningPath.why: Shows what changes when a task outlasts one context window: progress files, feature lists, one tested increment per session.

territories.title: The Peninsula of Long Thought
territories.subtitle: Planning and Reasoning
territories.about:
Planning and Reasoning covers how a model works its way to an answer instead of producing it in one shot. It starts with chain-of-thought: asking the model to write out intermediate steps before answering turned out to unlock multi-step math and logic in large models. Variations followed quickly. Self-consistency samples several chains and takes the majority answer, and program-aided reasoning has the model write code so an interpreter does the arithmetic.

A single chain can't recover from an early mistake, so the next step was search. Tree of Thoughts and its descendants treat partial reasoning as states to expand, score and backtrack from, and process reward models score each step so the search knows where to go. Planning researchers pushed further toward external checking: in LLM-Modulo systems the model only proposes plans and formal verifiers decide whether they are valid.

Since late 2024 much of this has moved inside the model. Reasoning models are trained with reinforcement learning to think at length before answering, and test-time compute became a dial: more thinking or more samples for a better answer at higher cost and latency. Landmarks worth knowing: chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree search, process reward models, and reasoning models. Open questions are whether the visible reasoning reflects what the model actually computed, which matters for anyone relying on it to monitor behavior, and whether reasoning will move out of text into hidden vectors.

learningPath.title: Stanford CS25: V5 I Large Language Model Reasoning, Denny Zhou of Google Deepmind
learningPath.why: One of the people behind chain-of-thought and self-consistency explains why intermediate steps help and how sampling, aggregation and RL fine-tuning build on that, which gives you the frame for everything in this region.

learningPath.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
learningPath.why: The paper that showed a few worked examples with written-out steps make large models much better at math and logic problems. Most later techniques here start from it.

learningPath.title: Why We Think
learningPath.why: A single long survey of test-time thinking: parallel sampling, sequential revision, search, reward models, latent thinking and faithfulness, with the papers behind each, so the node-level reading has somewhere to land.

learningPath.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
learningPath.why: Measures when spending more compute at answer time (search against a verifier, or revising answers) beats using a bigger model, and shows the best strategy depends on how hard the question is.

learningPath.title: Understanding Reasoning LLMs
learningPath.why: Explains how reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 are actually built (inference-time scaling, pure RL, SFT plus RL, distillation) in plain terms, which connects the prompting techniques above to today's trained thinkers.

learningPath.title: LLM-Modulo Frameworks as Compound AI Architectures for Robust Planning (& Reasoning)
learningPath.why: The skeptic's case: LLMs alone don't plan reliably, so pair them with external verifiers and solvers. Useful for deciding when to trust a model's plan and when to check it.

territories.title: The Tempering Grounds
territories.subtitle: Adaptation and Post-Training
territories.about:
Adaptation and Post-Training covers everything done to a model's weights after pretraining. Pretraining produces a model that continues text; post-training turns it into an assistant that follows instructions, matches a style, behaves safely, or reasons through hard problems. Prompting and retrieval change what a model sees, while this region changes the model itself.

The classic recipe, popularized by InstructGPT, has three stages: supervised fine-tuning on example answers, a reward model trained on human comparisons, and reinforcement learning (PPO) against that reward. It works but runs several models at once, and most later methods simplify it. DPO trains directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers with no reward model or RL loop, and spawned variants for unpaired thumbs-up data (KTO), single-stage training (ORPO), and fresh samples from the model being trained (online DPO). Constitutional AI replaced much of the human labeling with AI feedback. Reasoning models brought RL back: RL with verifiable rewards scores answers with checkers such as unit tests, and GRPO drops PPO's critic model to make that affordable. Distillation then passes the resulting skills on to small models.

For application teams, the practical tools are parameter-efficient. LoRA trains small add-on matrices instead of the full model, QLoRA does so over a 4-bit base on a single GPU, and DoRA and ReFT push efficiency further. Model merging combines fine-tunes by weight arithmetic with no training at all. Landmarks worth knowing: SFT, LoRA, RLHF, DPO, RLVR with GRPO, and distillation.

territories.title: The Quarries
territories.subtitle: Data and Synthetic Data
territories.about:
Data and Synthetic Data is about making the datasets an AI system is tested, tuned and trained on. For an application team that mostly means two things. The first is a golden set: real requests and known failures, labeled by someone who knows the domain, that every change is tested against. The second is a data flywheel that keeps that set, and any fine-tuning data, growing from production traces and user feedback. Models now do much of the labeling, with people reviewing samples and hard cases.

When real data runs short, models generate it. Self-Instruct showed in 2022 that a model can write an entire instruction dataset from a handful of seed tasks; Evol-Instruct made the generated tasks harder, and instruction backtranslation grounded them in human-written text. The same idea now produces RAG test questions from a company's own documents and, for agents, whole sandboxed tasks with automatic checks whose successful runs become training data. Generated data needs filtering as much as generating: near-duplicates, wrong answers and easy examples are thrown out, and a few thousand well-chosen examples often beat a much larger set.

Under this sits corpus hygiene, mostly the work of labs training base models: removing duplicates, filtering web text for quality, scrubbing personal information, and keeping test questions out of training data. A recurring worry is model collapse, where models trained only on earlier models' output lose rare knowledge over generations; keeping real data in the mix and checking generated examples against tests or solvers avoids it in practice. Landmarks worth knowing: golden sets, LLM-assisted labeling, the data flywheel, Self-Instruct, and decontamination.

learningPath.why: Shows how a team builds its first eval set from real traces, unit-style checks and human review, using one product as the running example. Start here because the golden set is what every other dataset in this region gets measured against.

territories.title: The Watchtowers
territories.subtitle: Evaluation and Observability
territories.about:
Evaluation and Observability is how teams find out whether an AI system works, and why it doesn't. Old NLP metrics like BLEU and ROUGE counted word overlap with a reference answer, which says nothing about whether an open-ended answer is right, so the field rebuilt measurement around benchmarks, human preference votes, and, above all, models grading other models.

LLM-as-a-judge is the region's center. A strong model with a rubric agrees with human raters about as often as humans agree with each other, which made evaluation cheap enough to run on every change. Most of what surrounds it is about making judges trustworthy: swapping answer order to cancel position bias, reading score probabilities instead of a single number, training small dedicated judge models, and using a few human labels to correct a judge's aggregate score. Specialized evals grew out of this for RAG (was the right context found, and is the answer grounded in it?), for long context (can the model find a needle in a haystack?), and for agents, where benchmarks like SWE-bench check whether a task got done and trajectory evals grade the steps along the way.

The engineering side borrows from software practice. Eval-driven development runs eval suites in CI the way tests gate code, layering cheap deterministic checks under model-graded ones. Tracing records each model call, retrieval and tool call as spans, now with shared OpenTelemetry conventions, and online evaluation scores sampled production traffic to catch drift. Landmarks worth knowing: capability and agent benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge, RAG evaluation, eval-driven development, and tracing.

territories.title: The Bulwark
territories.subtitle: Safety and Security
territories.about:
Safety and Security covers keeping AI systems from causing harm, whether through attacks, mistakes or misuse. Early on that meant filtering offensive output. Once models could read outside content and take actions, it became a security field: prompt injection showed that any text a model reads can act as an instruction, and agents with tools turned that into a way to leak data or take actions for an attacker.

Defenses come in layers because none is complete. Guardrails screen what goes in and out. Injection defenses help the model tell instructions from data, by training it to rank sources by privilege (the instruction hierarchy), by marking untrusted text (spotlighting), or by designing the system so the model that reads untrusted text cannot act (the dual LLM pattern). Sandboxing and scoped permissions limit how much damage a hijacked agent can do. Red teaming, increasingly automated with attacker models, looks for the gaps before release.

Interpretability is starting to become a control tool as well as a research field. Sparse autoencoders and representation engineering find concepts inside a model's activations, and circuit breakers and unlearning act on them directly. Landmarks worth knowing: prompt injection and its indirect form, guardrails, agent sandboxing, and red teaming.

territories.title: The New Agora
territories.subtitle: AI Product and Interaction Design
territories.about:
AI Product and Interaction Design is about how AI reaches people: the screens, conversations and controls that sit between a model and its user. It grew out of HCI work on mixed-initiative systems, and Microsoft's 2019 guidelines for human-AI interaction still frame the basics: set expectations, explain behavior, make correction cheap.

The modern era began with two surfaces. Copilots (2021) put suggestions inline where users already work, and chat (2022) made a message thread the default way to talk to a model. Streaming made replies feel fast, and citations let users check grounded answers. Chat's linear thread is a poor place to build something, so canvases and artifacts moved the work product into an editable pane beside the conversation, and generative UI lets the model answer with interface components instead of prose.

Agents shifted the focus from what the model says to what it does. Approval gates pause before consequential actions, plan previews let users fix a plan before work starts, and action traces show what actually happened. Recent studies find that reviewing only an agent's final result misses errors made early in the run, which is pushing products toward step-level visibility and steering. Reasoning models added a visible thinking panel, which helps users follow along but is not a faithful explanation of how the answer was reached.

Landmarks worth knowing: the human-AI interaction guidelines, chat, copilots, citations, and human-in-the-loop approval. The open problem is trust calibration: getting users to rely on AI when it is right and check it when it is not, as outputs become longer, more autonomous and harder to verify.

territories.title: The Painted Isles
territories.subtitle: Multimodal
territories.about:
Multimodal covers AI that works with images, audio, video and documents, not just text. It started with alignment: CLIP (2021) trained image and text encoders so a picture and its caption land close together, giving models a shared vocabulary for both. Vision-language models then fed those image vectors into a language model as extra tokens, and training on visual instructions turned them into assistants that read screenshots, charts and photos. Later models take images at their native resolution, which made small text and dense layouts readable, and sample frames to follow video.

Documents were one of the first places this paid off. Pipelines that chain layout detection and OCR lose reading order and garble tables, so vision models that read a whole page and output structured text are replacing them, and visual retrieval such as ColPali searches page images directly. Speech went the same way. Whisper made transcription a commodity, audio language models turned sound into tokens a language model can predict, and realtime voice moved from slow recognize-think-speak chains to single models that hear and speak audio, some of them listening and talking at once.

Generation runs on a separate line. Diffusion models create images by removing noise step by step; latent diffusion made text-to-image practical, transformers replaced the U-Net inside, and flow matching cut the number of steps. The same machinery, applied to patches across space and time, produces video. Landmarks worth knowing: CLIP, vision-language models, document understanding, Whisper, realtime voice, and latent diffusion. The open problems are mostly practical: images and audio use many tokens, so cost and latency dominate design, and generated video and speech still need better control.

territories.title: The Clockwork Isle
territories.subtitle: Embodied AI and World Models
territories.about:
Embodied AI is about models that act in the physical world, or that simulate it well enough to train in. Classical robotics planned every motion explicitly and broke whenever the scene differed from what its engineers expected. The modern approach learns a policy, a model that maps camera images and an instruction to motor commands, from demonstrations, simulation and large pretrained models.

The field moved fast after 2022. Language models first entered as planners that picked from a robot's fixed list of skills (SayCan) or wrote code against its control API. Then vision-language-action models (RT-2, OpenVLA, π0) fine-tuned a vision-language model to output actions directly. How to output those actions became the central design question: discrete tokens were coarse, diffusion policies handled demonstrations that do a task several ways but were slow, and flow-matching action heads made smooth, high-rate control practical. Most current systems split the work: a slow vision-language model reasons about the scene a few times a second while a fast action policy drives the motors.

The hard limit is data. Robot demonstrations are expensive, so teams pool data across robot types, collect it with cheap teleoperation rigs, pretrain on human video, and train in simulation, increasingly with generated images or interactive world models standing in for the real world. Landmarks worth knowing: sim-to-real transfer, diffusion policy, action chunking, VLAs, and cross-embodiment training. The open problems are reliability outside the lab, evaluating policies without running them on real robots, and pushing past what imitation alone can teach, with reinforcement learning fine-tuning as the current bet.

territories.title: The Chancery
territories.subtitle: Governance and Compliance
territories.about:
The Governance and Compliance region covers what an AI team owes to people outside it: regulators, auditors, customers, the public and the owners of the data it trains on. It began with documentation. Model cards (2018) set out what a model is for, how it was evaluated and where it fails, and today's system cards, often running to hundreds of pages, grew out of them.

From 2023 the voluntary principles turned into frameworks and law. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework gave teams a shared process for finding and managing risk, ISO/IEC 42001 made it certifiable, and the EU AI Act (in force from 2024, with duties phasing in through 2027) made it binding for high-risk systems and general-purpose models. The EU's Code of Practice then spelled out what model providers actually have to produce: a standard documentation form, a copyright policy that honors crawler opt-outs, and for the largest models a safety and security framework with evaluations and incident reporting.

Frontier labs built their own rules for extreme risks. Dangerous-capability evaluations test whether a model could help with bioweapons or cyberattacks or act autonomously, and frontier safety frameworks such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy commit the lab to stronger safeguards, or a pause, once a threshold is crossed. In August 2026 OpenAI paused RL training for two weeks after it could not rule out that Astra had reached its Critical cyber threshold. Critics point out that the labs write and enforce these rules themselves.

Two further problems involve what models consume and produce. Content provenance (C2PA) signs media with a record of how it was made, though the metadata is easily stripped, so it is paired with watermarks. On the input side, audits found widespread license errors in training datasets and a fast rise in sites blocking AI crawlers, which pushed teams toward tracking licenses and buying data. Landmarks worth knowing: model cards, the NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, frontier safety frameworks and C2PA.

landmarks.desc: Probabilistic ranking function scoring documents by term frequency and inverse document frequency; the standard lexical search baseline.
landmarks.summary: Scores how well a document matches a query from the query words it contains: rare words count more, repeats help with diminishing returns, and long documents aren't rewarded just for being long. Tuned in the Okapi system in the early 1990s, it is still the default ranking in Lucene and Elasticsearch and the lexical half of most hybrid search behind RAG.

landmarks.maturityNote: Every production LLM uses a subword tokenizer; engineers meet it as token counting and cost.

landmarks.name: Rotary Position Embeddings
landmarks.maturityNote: The default position encoding in Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek and most open models.

landmarks.name: Sparse Attention
landmarks.maturityNote: In production in DeepSeek-V3.2 (DSA) and Kimi (MoBA); most open models still use dense attention.
landmarks.desc: Letting each query attend to a small, learned selection of earlier tokens or blocks instead of all of them, trained into the model so long contexts cost far less compute.

landmarks.name: Autoregressive Decoding
landmarks.maturityNote: The baseline execution pattern of every generative model.
landmarks.desc: Generating text one token at a time, each conditioned on everything generated so far, using a sampling strategy.
landmarks.summary: A language model writes one token at a time. It scores every possible next token, a sampling rule (greedy, temperature, top-p) picks one, and that token is appended and fed back in. Every new token needs another pass through the whole model, and that pass is limited mostly by how fast weights and cached state can be read from memory, not by arithmetic. landmarks.name: KV Cache
landmarks.maturityNote: Non-negotiable serving infrastructure.
landmarks.desc: Storing attention keys and values from earlier tokens so each decoding step avoids recomputation; its memory footprint dominates serving design.
landmarks.summary: During generation, attention needs the keys and values of every earlier token. The KV cache stores them, so each step computes them only for the new token instead of reprocessing the whole sequence. The catch is memory: the cache grows with every token and every concurrent request, and for long contexts it can outgrow the model weights, so most serving design is about fitting, sharing and shrinking it.

landmarks.name: PagedAttention
landmarks.maturityNote: Dominant memory-management approach in serving engines.
landmarks.desc: Stores the KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks, like OS virtual memory, cutting fragmentation and raising batch sizes.
landmarks.summary: Stores each request's KV cache in small fixed-size blocks scattered across GPU memory and tracked by a block table, the way an operating system pages virtual memory. Engines no longer reserve one large contiguous region per request for its maximum length, so far less memory is wasted and many more requests fit in a batch. landmarks.name: Speculative Decoding
landmarks.maturityNote: Broadly integrated into serving engines; draft-head variants (EAGLE, Medusa) are now the common form.
landmarks.desc: A small draft model or head proposes several tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, reducing latency without changing outputs.

landmarks.name: Prompt Caching
landmarks.maturityNote: Offered by major API providers; shapes how prompts are structured.
landmarks.desc: Reusing the computed KV cache for shared prompt prefixes across requests, cutting prefill cost and latency.

landmarks.name: Grouped-Query Attention
landmarks.maturityNote: Used by most open-weight models; well-understood quality and memory tradeoff.

landmarks.maturityNote: In production at large providers; open tooling (LMCache, Dynamo, llm-d) still settling.
landmarks.desc: Moving KV cache out of GPU memory into CPU memory, SSD or a shared networked pool, so cached prefixes survive GPU eviction and can be reused across machines.

landmarks.name: Semantic Caching
landmarks.maturityNote: Offered by gateways and vector databases; correctness of loose matches limits it to repetitive, low-stakes traffic.

landmarks.name: Tensor, Pipeline and Expert Parallelism
landmarks.maturityNote: Assumed by every multi-GPU serving engine; the right mix for MoE models is still tuned case by case.
landmarks.desc: Splitting one model across many GPUs, by slicing each layer's matrices (tensor), assigning layers to stages (pipeline), or placing MoE experts on different devices (expert).
landmarks.summary: A large model doesn't fit on one GPU, so it is split. Tensor parallelism cuts each layer's weight matrices across GPUs that work in lockstep and needs fast links, so it stays within one server. Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU a block of layers and passes activations along, which works across servers. Expert parallelism puts different mixture-of-experts experts on different GPUs. landmarks.name: Diffusion Language Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Commercial models (Mercury, Gemini Diffusion) and open ones (LLaDA, Dream) exist; frontier models remain autoregressive.
landmarks.desc: Generating text by starting from a fully masked sequence and unmasking many tokens in parallel over a few refinement steps, instead of one token at a time left to right.

A diffusion language model starts with a block of blank (masked) tokens and fills them in over a handful of passes, committing many tokens per pass and revising as it goes. Quality has caught up for code and short tasks but not yet at the frontier, and serving engines are still built around autoregressive decoding.

landmarks.name: Late Interaction
landmarks.maturityNote: Supported natively by Vespa, Qdrant and others and used in production, but single-vector search remains the default; index size is the main cost.

landmarks.summary: Ordinary vector search squeezes a whole passage into one vector, which blurs detail. Late interaction keeps one vector per token, and scores a passage by finding, for each word of the question, its best-matching word in the passage and adding those scores up. A transformer reads a passage and outputs a weight for each vocabulary word, including related words that never appear in the text, so a passage about "cars" can match "automobile". landmarks.name: Embedding Compression
landmarks.maturityNote: Supported by major embedding APIs (OpenAI text-embedding-3 dimensions parameter) and vector databases.

landmarks.name: On-Policy Distillation
landmarks.maturityNote: Used in the post-training of recent small open models such as Qwen3's; supported in common training libraries.
landmarks.desc: Distillation in which the student generates its own outputs and the teacher scores each token, so the student learns to recover from its own mistakes.
landmarks.summary: Ordinary distillation trains the student on text the teacher wrote, but at use time the student reads its own output, and one early slip can lead it somewhere the teacher's examples never went. In on-policy distillation the student writes its own answers and the teacher grades every token, so the student learns from the mistakes it actually makes. landmarks.name: Continued Pretraining
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard route to domain and language models; recipes to avoid forgetting are well documented.
landmarks.desc: Resuming next-token pretraining on a large unlabeled corpus from a new domain or language before instruction tuning, to teach knowledge and vocabulary that fine-tuning can't.
landmarks.summary: Fine-tuning teaches a model how to behave, but it is a poor way to teach a lot of new knowledge. Continued pretraining runs the original next-token training on billions of tokens of domain text (code, medicine, finance, a new language) and then re-applies instruction tuning. It is how most domain models are built; the main risk is forgetting general skills, which is managed by mixing in general data and keeping the learning rate low.

landmarks.maturityNote: How frontier agentic and coding models are trained; open frameworks and hosted RL fine-tuning bring it to smaller teams.
landmarks.desc: Training a model with reinforcement learning over whole multi-step episodes in which it calls tools and sees their results, rewarded on whether the task was completed.
landmarks.summary: Reasoning RL rewards a single answer. Agentic RL rewards a whole episode: the model searches, runs code or edits files, reads the results, and keeps going until the task is done or fails, and the outcome is scored. landmarks.maturityNote: Order swapping and length control are built into common eval tools and leaderboards; self-preference is harder to remove.

landmarks.name: Spotlighting
landmarks.maturityNote: Delimiting untrusted text is common practice; datamarking and encoding are less widely adopted.
landmarks.desc: Transforming untrusted text before it reaches the model (delimiting it, interleaving a marker, or encoding it) so the model can see which text is data and not follow it.
landmarks.summary: Untrusted text such as a retrieved web page is transformed before it goes into the prompt so the model can tell it apart from instructions. The simplest version wraps it in delimiters; stronger ones put a special marker between every word (datamarking) or encode the whole text, and the system prompt says never to follow instructions inside marked text. landmarks.name: Dual LLM Pattern
landmarks.maturityNote: A widely cited design; production systems mostly use partial versions of it.
landmarks.desc: Splitting an assistant into a privileged model that calls tools but never sees untrusted text, and a quarantined model that reads untrusted text but cannot act, with ordinary code passing references between them.
landmarks.summary: An architecture for assistants that must read untrusted content. A privileged model takes the user's instructions and calls tools but never sees untrusted text; a quarantined model reads that text (a web page, an email) but has no tools. Plain code between them hands the quarantined model's output to tools as opaque variables, so injected instructions have nothing to trigger. Google DeepMind's CaMeL (2025) builds the idea into a working system. The cost is extra complexity and fewer tasks the assistant can do.

landmarks.maturityNote: The backbone of most current image and video generators.

A diffusion transformer cuts the latent image into patches and processes them as tokens, like a vision transformer, so quality keeps rising with model size and compute. landmarks.name: Flow Matching
landmarks.maturityNote: The default objective for many 2024+ generators; diffusion remains common.
landmarks.desc: Training a generator to follow a learned velocity field from noise to data, usually along straight paths, instead of learning to reverse a noising process.
landmarks.summary: An alternative training objective to diffusion. Instead of learning to remove noise step by step, the model learns which direction to move at each point to get from noise to an image, with the paths kept close to straight lines. Straighter paths need fewer sampling steps, and training is simpler. Recent image, video and speech models such as Stable Diffusion 3 and Flux use it.

landmarks.desc: Vision-language models trained on large amounts of 3D spatial question answering so they can estimate distances, sizes and positions in a scene, not just name what's in it.

Spatial reasoning VLMs are trained on millions of generated questions about distances, sizes and relative positions, built from images with estimated depth. landmarks.maturityNote: Mainstream in creative tools and open-model communities; zero-shot reference methods are catching up.
landmarks.desc: Teaching an image model a specific subject or style from a handful of photos by fine-tuning it, today usually as a small LoRA, then generating that subject in new scenes.

Fine-tuning an image model on three to twenty pictures binds them to a new word, after which prompts can put that subject anywhere. landmarks.maturityNote: Shipped in ChatGPT and Gemini and open models such as BAGEL and Janus; most dedicated image pipelines still use separate diffusion models.
landmarks.desc: One model that both understands and generates text and images in the same sequence, so it can draw, edit and explain within a conversation.

Unified models read and produce both: image tokens or image patches share one sequence with text, so the model draws with everything it knows from the conversation. To keep them from depending on the simulator's clean look and exact physics, engineers randomize textures, lighting, masses and friction during training, so the real world becomes just one more variation the policy has already seen. landmarks.desc: Learning a compact model of how an environment changes in response to actions, then training a policy inside that learned model instead of the real environment.

A policy can then practice inside this learned model, imagining thousands of trajectories, and needs far fewer trials in the real environment. Here it acts as the planner: it breaks an instruction into steps and either picks each one from the robot's list of skills, checking that the skill can succeed in the current scene (SayCan), or writes a short program against the robot's control API (Code as Policies). landmarks.name: Diffusion Policy
landmarks.maturityNote: A default baseline for imitation learning; flow-matching heads are replacing it where speed matters.
landmarks.desc: Generating robot actions with a denoising diffusion model conditioned on observations, which captures demonstrations that have several valid ways to do the task.
landmarks.summary: People demonstrate the same task in different ways, for example reaching around a cup from the left one time and from the right the next. A model trained to predict the average action would reach straight into the cup. A diffusion policy generates the next stretch of actions by denoising, as image generators do, so it commits to one valid way instead of averaging them. It became the default for learning from demonstrations, at the cost of several model passes per action.

Its policy, ACT, predicts a chunk of the next few dozen actions at once instead of one step at a time, which keeps motion smooth and stops small errors from piling up. Because the base model already knows what objects are and what words mean, the robot can follow instructions it was never shown, like 'move the banana to the picture of Germany'. landmarks.maturityNote: The action head of several leading open and commercial VLAs; discrete tokenizers remain a competing choice.

landmarks.desc: Tests of whether a model can meaningfully help with severe harms — bioweapons, cyberattacks, autonomous replication, undermining oversight — run before release to decide what safeguards it needs.

landmarks.name: Frontier Safety Frameworks
landmarks.maturityNote: Published by every major frontier lab and referenced by law (EU Code of Practice, California SB 53). In August 2026 OpenAI paused RL training for two weeks after it could not rule out that Astra had reached its framework's Critical cyber threshold, the first publicly reported trigger of this kind.
landmarks.desc: A lab's published commitment that sets capability thresholds, says how they are measured, and names the safeguards required before a model that crosses one can be trained further or deployed.
landmarks.summary: A frontier lab's published if-then commitment: if testing shows a model has crossed a defined danger threshold, then specific security and deployment safeguards must be in place before it is trained further or released. Anthropic's AI Safety Levels, OpenAI's High and Critical tiers and Google DeepMind's Critical Capability Levels all work this way. landmarks.name: Content Provenance and Credentials
landmarks.maturityNote: Built into major image generators, cameras and some platforms; metadata is easily stripped, so it is paired with watermarks.
landmarks.desc: Attaching cryptographically signed metadata to media that records who or what made it and how it was edited, so viewers can check whether an image, video or audio clip was generated by AI.
landmarks.summary: A signed record attached to an image, video or audio file that says who or what made it and how it was edited. The C2PA standard bundles these claims into a manifest, signs it with a certificate and binds it to the file's exact bytes, so any viewer can check it offline. Its weakness is that many tools silently strip the metadata, so it is usually paired with invisible watermarks that survive re-encoding.

landmarks.name: Training Data Licensing and Opt-Outs
landmarks.maturityNote: Opt-out controls and licensing deals are now routine for large crawls; the legal ground (fair use, text-and-data-mining exceptions) is still being decided in court.
landmarks.desc: Tracking where training data came from, under what license, and whether its owners opted out, so a team knows what it may legally train on.
landmarks.summary: Knowing where training data came from, what license it carries and whether its owners have opted out of AI training. Audits found that dataset licenses are often wrong or missing, and that a large share of the best web sources now block AI crawlers in robots.txt. Teams respond by tracking the license of every source, honoring opt-outs and buying licensed data, while courts are still deciding how copyright applies.

landmarks.name: AI Bill of Materials
landmarks.maturityNote: Formats exist (CycloneDX ML-BOM, SPDX 3.0 AI) and government guidance appeared in 2026; tooling and adoption are early.
landmarks.desc: A machine-readable inventory of what an AI system is built from — models and their lineage, datasets and their licenses, code dependencies and pipelines — in a software bill of materials format.
landmarks.summary: A machine-readable parts list for an AI system: which models (with weight hashes and what they were fine-tuned from), which datasets and licenses, which libraries and pipelines. It extends the software bill of materials that security teams already use, so the same tools can flag a vulnerable dependency or a problem license. Critics note that it lists components but not what an agent is allowed to do at runtime.

landmarks.name: AI Impact Assessments
landmarks.maturityNote: Mandatory under the EU AI Act for some deployers from August 2026; templates and practice are still forming.
landmarks.desc: A documented review, before deployment, of how an AI system could affect the people it is used on — discrimination, loss of rights, harm to vulnerable groups — and what oversight and mitigations will address it.
landmarks.summary: A written review, done before an AI system goes live, of how it could affect the people it makes decisions about: who could be treated unfairly, what rights are at stake, and what human oversight and complaint routes exist. The EU AI Act requires one (a fundamental rights impact assessment) from certain deployers of high-risk systems such as public bodies, banks and insurers. It works like a GDPR data protection impact assessment, widened from privacy to all fundamental rights.
